fact_checks.claim: Since 2026-03-01 the Free plan is 1 user and cannot create a team (previously up to 3).
fact_checks.correction: Postman docs say plans 'changed in March 2026'. Free 'is limited to one user' and 'can't create a team'. Before that, Free teams could have 'up to three users'. Postman gives no exact day. March 1 matches the first stable v12 build (12.0.1, 2026-03-01) and third-party reports. Legacy Basic and Professional plans stay as they are until renewal. Postman does not say what happens to existing 3-user Free teams.

fact_checks.claim: Collection runs and mock server usage have been unlimited on all plans since March 2026.
fact_checks.correction: Docs: 'Collection runs are now unlimited on all plans' and 'Mock server usage is now unlimited on all plans', as part of the March 2026 changes. Exception: legacy plans stay limited 'based on plan type' until renewal. The pricing page lists 'Automated API testing (Unlimited, Collection Runner)' and mock servers on all four tiers. Monitoring is still metered.

fact_checks.claim: Paid tiers: Solo $9/month and Team $19/user/month (annual billing). Enterprise is 'contact sales'; the public $49 price was removed around 2026-09-19.
fact_checks.verdict: confirmed for prices and contact sales; unverified for the $49 removal date
fact_checks.correction: The pricing page shows '$9 per month (billed annually)' and '$19 per user/month (billed annually)'. Monthly-billing prices are not shown (a toggle says annual saves 'up to 25%'). Enterprise reads 'Contact sales for pricing' and no $49 appears anywhere. No Postman page dates a removal of a $49 price, and the Wayback Machine could not be fetched. The only $49 Enterprise figure found was in a third-party article syndicated from Apidog (Barchart).

fact_checks.claim: Free plan: 50 AI credits/month, 1,000 monitor requests/month, 25 Flows credits/month.
fact_checks.correction: Exact labels: 50 AI credits/month (no overage on Free), 1,000 monitoring requests/month per team, and 25 'Automation Flows' credits/month. Manual Flows have no cap. Free also includes 10,000 Postman API calls/month, up to 5 integrations, and a 1-day collection recovery window.

fact_checks.claim: Scratch Pad was removed on Sep 15, 2023; signed-out users get only the Lightweight API Client, without collections or environments.
fact_checks.correction: Docs only say 'Scratch Pad is no longer available in Postman v10.18 and later' (deprecated, no updates). A search snippet of the help center dates it to September 2023. The 15 Sep date appears only in a forum post. Signed out, the lightweight API Client works offline and stores everything locally. It sends HTTP, WebSocket, Socket.IO, GraphQL, gRPC and MQTT requests, keeps history, and runs post-response scripts and the visualizer. Collections, environments and variables are documented only 'when you're in a workspace', which needs sign-in. So 'no collections or environments' is implied, not stated outright.

fact_checks.claim: Newman is no longer maintained and cannot run Collection v3 (YAML).
fact_checks.correction: Postman docs: 'Newman is no longer maintained.' and 'It isn't compatible with the collection v3 format used in Postman v12 and later, which is the only collection format supported in Native Git workflows.' Postman tells users to move to the Postman CLI. Newman still runs v2.1 JSON collections. The GitHub repo has no archive banner or deprecation notice.

fact_checks.claim: Postman v12 reached GA on 2026-03-01 with Native Git and Collection v3 YAML; Postbot was removed.
fact_checks.correction: Postman's stable app changelog lists 12.0.1 at 2026-03-01T05:25Z. Its notes introduce Native Git, 'the Collection 3.0 format' (collections 'broken into constituent YAML files') and local mock servers. They also state 'Postbot is no longer available in Postman v12' and point to Agent Mode instead. The first stable v12 build listed is 12.0.1, not 12.0.0, and Postman does not use the term 'GA'. The postman.com/release-notes page showed no version entries.

fact_checks.claim: Postman has a desktop capture proxy and the Interceptor extension, but no documented rewrite, breakpoint or map-local tools.
fact_checks.correction: There is a third capture method: the Browser Tool (since 12.15.0), which captures a web app's calls and turns them into requests. The proxy handles HTTP/HTTPS (devices need the Postman certificate), and Interceptor is a browser extension. Capture works in start/stop sessions with search, filter, save-to-collection and cookie sync. The capture docs mention no rewrite, breakpoints, pause/edit, map local, map remote, throttling or replay. The changelog entries checked (11.77.0 to 12.31.7) do not add any of these either.

fact_checks.claim: The Browser Tool arrived in 12.15.0 (2026-06-15), with Playwright test generation via Agent Mode.
fact_checks.correction: 12.15.0 (2026-06-15T02:54Z) is the earliest changelog entry for the Browser Tool ('Navigate web applications with the Postman Browser Tool'). It covers browsing inside Postman, logging network calls, turning them into requests, and 'use Agent Mode to automate browser workflows, generate tests'. Those notes do not name Playwright. Playwright appears alongside the Browser Tool and Agent Mode test generation in 12.20.1 (2026-07-21). It is also mentioned in 12.9.7 (2026-05-08), context not checked.

fact_checks.claim: CloudSEK (Dec 2024) found 30,000+ public Postman workspaces leaking secrets.
fact_checks.correction: CloudSEK's blog of Dec 23, 2024 (TRIAD team) reports 'more than 30,000 publicly accessible Postman workspaces' exposing access tokens, refresh tokens, third-party API keys and some PII. The findings come from a year-long XVigil investigation. Top services were GitHub (5,924) and Slack (5,552), though it is unclear whether these count workspaces or secrets. One case was a private workspace leaked through a vendor. This is CloudSEK's research, not a Postman disclosure.

missing: Browser Tool (12.15.0+): a built-in browser that logs a web app's API calls, turns them into requests, and lets Agent Mode automate flows and generate tests. This overlaps directly with our browser-capture flow.

Collection v3 YAML with Native Git: one YAML file per request, kept in the user's own repo and editable offline. The Postman CLI's run, migrate (v2.1 to v3) and lint commands replace Newman. We need v3 YAML import/export to work with Postman users.

Local mock servers (12.0.1) with unlimited mock usage: users expect offline mocking. Combining mocks with rewrite, breakpoint and map-local rules would set us apart, since Postman documents none of these.

No-login, local-only client that covers HTTP, WebSocket, Socket.IO, GraphQL, gRPC and MQTT, with history, post-response scripts and a visualizer. This is the minimum users expect for protocol coverage and offline use.

Secret safety and free sharing: the CloudSEK leaks show a need to detect and redact secrets before export or sharing. The 1-user Free plan leaves small teams wanting free collaboration, for example through Git. Syncing captured cookies into a cookie jar is also expected.
errors: All 20 tool calls were used. WebFetch cannot reach the Wayback Machine, so the date the $49 Enterprise price was removed could not be checked. postman.com/release-notes showed no version list, so I used Postman's official changelog feed on dl.pstmn.io instead. Only characters 0 to 200k of about 453k were read, covering 11.77.0 to 12.31.7. The blog.postman.com post on the Scratch Pad sunset returned 404. WebFetch returns model-written summaries, so quotes are as extracted and not raw page text.
